newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS - Mixed views on Handelsbanken bid.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Mixed views on Handelsbanken bid.

text.p: Analysts were divided on Friday on the benefits of Sweden's Handelsbanken launching a cash takeover bid for mortgage bank Stadshypotek that is also being wooed by insurer Skandia.
"The net effect is mainly negative, but the deal is strategically and structurally correct," Fredrik Myren, analyst at HSBC James Capel, told Reuters.
On the negative side, analysts noted that if the 22.9 billion crown ($3.37 billion) deal went through, the bank would have a very low capital ratio.
Furthermore, synergies would be delayed as the bank only intended to reduce staff through natural wastage and there would be merger costs not yet been taken into account.

But other analysts focused on the bank expanding core operations, increasing income, becoming Scandinavia's largest bank and blocking rivals from getting Stadshypotek, Sweden's largest mortgage lender with a third of the market.
Handelsbanken launched the bid for Stadshypotek on Thursday an dif it was successful would give it a dominant 40 percent slice of Sweden's mortgage market.

The bid was given an initial nod of approval by the state, which is Stadshypotek's largest single owner with a 34 percent stake, on the condition that no higher offers are received during an ongoing process to auction its holding.

On Friday, U.S. credit ratings agency Standard & Poor's put Handelsbanken on creditwatch with negative implications, adding that "the reduced level of capital will make the bank one of the lowest capitalised banks in Europe".

The acquisition would depress Handelsbanken's total capital ratio to 8.5 percent, from a level of 12.1 percent at the end of September, and its core capital ratio to 4.8 percent, from 8.4 percent in September.
The core capital ratio will then be just somewhat higher than the allowed lower limit of four percent.
Analysts expected the new capital ratio figures to cause further downgradings from rating institutes.
But analysts positive to the deal dismissed the low capital ratio and possible downgradings.

"If Handelsbanken will have largely the same income level in 1997 and 1998 as in 1996, and if Stadshypotek does not lose 50 percent or more of its income, the total capital ratio will be more than 10 percent in 1998," an analyst said.
For the first nine months of 1996, Handelsbanken posted a profit after credit losses of 4.52 billion crowns. For calendar 1995 it posted a profit of 4.96 billion crowns.
The analysts saw Handelsbanken's share having a target price of around 200 crowns, give or take five crowns.
In late trade on Friday the share was trading 2.5 crowns lower at 193.5 crowns.
Others expected the share to slip as the low capital ratio will increase the risk premium on it.
"If the bid goes through, the share is likely to underperform the general index," Myren said.
Myren expected some restructuring costs to arise, while the bank had not calculated with any.
"Also, synergy effects will be delayed as the bank won't cut staff by other means than natural wastage," he said.
Several analysts expected sharedholders to accept the bid.

Insurer Skandia, which proposed a merger with Stadshypotek on November 25, said on Friday it was continuing to prepare a merger prospectus ahead of a related extraordinary shareholders' meeting on December 19.
The proposal, that valued Stadshypotek at around 21 billion crowns, has been fiercely opposed by the government which wants to get the highest possible price for its stake.
